summary.text: In Homer the father of Rhesus, king of the Thracians who came to Troy with the fairest horses the spy Dolon had ever seen — whiter than snow, and swift as the winds.

story.text: When Dolon, caught by Odysseus and Diomedes, betrayed the disposition of the allies, he named the Thracians under their king Rhesus son of Eïoneus — new comers, camped outermost of all, with horses fairer and swifter than any others in the host. So Homer gives Rhesus a mortal father and says nothing of a divine mother.

Apollodorus instead makes Rhesus the son of the river-god Strymon and the Muse Euterpe — or, as the same hand admits, of Calliope. The Eïoneus of the *Iliad* belongs to the epic's mortal frame; the Muse-and-river genealogy belongs to the mythographer's catalogue.

He is not the Eïoneus whom Hector slew in Book 7 beneath the well-wrought helm of bronze, nor Deioneus father of Cephalus in the older genealogies — only the Thracian father named in the night-raid episode.
